statements_en: The inequality $x^{2} - 2x + 2 \ge 0$ holds for all real x, and is never equal to 0.
The inequality $x^{2} + 5x - 14 > 0$ has solution set $x < -7$ or $x > 2$.
The inequality $x^{2} - 4x + 5 > 0$ holds for all real x.
The inequality $x^{2} - 11x + 30 < 0$ has solution set $(5, 6)$.
The inequality $x^{2} + 14x + 49 \ge 0$ holds for all real x, with equality at both $x = 7$ and $x = -7$.
tactical_explanations_en:
**A.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
(x^{2} - 2 x) + 2\ge 0
$$

Bring every term to one side.

$$
x^{2} - 2 x + 2\ge 0
$$

The discriminant is $-4$, so there are no real roots.

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 2 x + 2$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $+$ |

The solution set is

$$
(-\infty, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
(x^{2} + 5 x) - 14>0
$$

Factor.

$$
(x - 2) (x + 7)>0
$$

The roots are the critical points.

$$
x=-7
$$

$$
x=2
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x (x + 5) - 14$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-7)$ | $+$ |
| $(-7,2)$ | $-$ |
| $(2,\infty)$ | $+$ |

The solution set is

$$
(-\infty, -7) \cup (2, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
(x^{2} - 4 x) + 5>0
$$

Bring every term to one side.

$$
x^{2} - 4 x + 5>0
$$

The discriminant is $-4$, so there are no real roots.

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 4 x + 5$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $+$ |

The solution set is

$$
(-\infty, \infty)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Factor the quadratic, mark the roots, and test the sign on each interval. The claim starts from

$$
x^{2} - 11x + 30 < 0
$$

Factoring first:

$$
x^{2} - 11x + 30 = (x - 5)(x - 6)
$$

The critical points are the roots of the quadratic:

$$
x = 5,\quad x = 6
$$

The inequality is strict ($<$), so keep the middle region without its endpoints:

$$
(5, 6)
$$

Reading the signs on the open intervals made by the critical points:

| Interval | Sign |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty, 5)$ | $+$ |
| $(5, 6)$ | $-$ |
| $(6, \infty)$ | $+$ |

A quick check: plug in $x = 5.5$: 30.25 - 60.5 + 30 = -0.25 < 0, confirming it belongs.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Start from the claimed inequality.

$$
(x^{2} + 14 x) + 49\ge 0
$$

Factor.

$$
(x + 7)^{2}\ge 0
$$

The roots are the critical points.

$$
x=-7
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x (x + 14) + 49$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-7)$ | $+$ |
| $(-7,\infty)$ | $+$ |

The solution set is

$$
(-\infty, \infty)
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.

A compound inequality is two conditions that must hold together. Solve each piece, then intersect.

$$
-8\le (x^{2} - 12 x) + 30\le 4
$$

**Left piece.**

$$
-8\le (x^{2} - 12 x) + 30
$$

$$
x^{2} - 12 x + 38\ge 0
$$

So the left piece gives

$$
(-\infty, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 12 x) + 30\le 4
$$

$$
x^{2} - 12 x + 26\le 0
$$

$$
x=6 - \sqrt{10}
$$

$$
x=\sqrt{10} + 6
$$

Sign chart on the open intervals:

| Interval | Sign of $x^{2} - 12 x + 26$ |
| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,6 - \sqrt{10})$ | $+$ |
| $(6 - \sqrt{10},\sqrt{10} + 6)$ | $-$ |
| $(\sqrt{10} + 6,\infty)$ | $+$ |

So the right piece gives

$$
[6 - \sqrt{10}, \sqrt{10} + 6]
$$

Intersect both pieces.

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

$$
(-\infty, \infty)
$$

**Right piece.**

$$
(x^{2} - 14 x) + 40\le 3
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
x + 5\ge 0
$$

$$
x\in [-5, \infty)
$$

**Case when the non-radical side is negative.**

A square root is always $\ge 0$, so the inequality holds automatically on the part of the domain where the right side is negative.

**Case when the non-radical side is nonnegative.**

Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring preserves the inequality direction.

$$
x + 5>x^{2} - 2 x + 1
$$

$$
- x^{2} + 3 x + 4>0
$$

$$

$$

$$
x=-1

$$

| --- | --- |
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $-$ |

| $(4,\infty)$ | $-$ |

Intersecting the squared case with the domain and the sign case gives

$$
[-5, 4)
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Start from the absolute-value sum inequality.

$$
|x - 2|+|x + 3|\le 7
$$

The expression changes formula at the kink points $x=-3$ and $x=2$.

On $x\le -3$:

$$
|x - 2|+|x + 3|=- 2 x - 1
$$

Solving $- 2 x - 1\le 7$ on this piece gives

$$
[-4, -3]
$$

On $-3\le x\le 2$:

$$
|x - 2|+|x + 3|=5
$$

Solving $5\le 7$ on this piece gives

$$
[-3, 2]
$$

On $x\ge 2$:

$$
|x - 2|+|x + 3|=2 x + 1
$$

Solving $2 x + 1\le 7$ on this piece gives

$$
[2, 3]
$$

Union of the admissible pieces:

$$
[-4, 3]
$$

which matches the claimed set.

So the statement is True.
